items.title: ECHO: A Longitudinal Study of Contextual Consistency and Alignment Limits in Large Language Models
items.abstract: ECHO (Evaluation of Contextual Consistency and Alignment Limits in Large Language Models) is a longitudinal research project investigating contextual retention, narrative coherence, corrective learning, and alignment limitations in Large Language Models (LLMs). The study is based on approximately 900 hours of human-AI interaction conducted over 90 consecutive days under real-world usage conditions. Unlike traditional benchmark evaluations focused on isolated tasks, ECHO analyzes long-term conversational behavior, contextual fidelity, adaptation to corrective feedback, and degradation patterns in extended interactions. The project also introduces the Contextual Fidelity Index (CFI), a proposed framework for evaluating contextual consistency in conversational AI systems. Research Areas: Artificial Intelligence Human-AI Interaction Computational Linguistics Cognitive Science Human-Centered AI Prompt Engineering Principal Investigator: Valtemar Siani

items.title: EdFitter: a hybrid course recommendation system using large language models
items.abstract: Educational institutions face increasing pressure to adapt their curricula to the rapidly evolving demands of the job market, and recommender systems can be important tools to guide students in selecting courses that align with their career goals. We present EdFitter, a hybrid course recommendation system that combines pretrained text embeddings for retrieval with large language models (LLMs) used offline for semantic skill extraction. The system is designed for a cold-start setting in which free-text job queries must be matched to a university’s institutional course catalog. Instead of relying on direct generative recommendations, EdFitter ranks stored course descriptions by cosine similarity and augments the output with extracted skills and matching vacancy examples. We evaluate the system in a pilot institutional deployment at Higher School of Economics (HSE) using a multi-level study with student respondents, controlled assessors, and interviews with program directors. The results indicate that users perceive the recommendations as sufficiently relevant and potentially useful to justify further development. Overall, the study suggests that EdFitter is a valuable tool for supporting course exploration and curriculum-to-labor-market alignment; we also highlight important limitations and directions for future work.

items.title: Effect of an Occupational Health and Safety Educational Intervention on Knowledge, Practices, Musculoskeletal Disorders, and Injuries Among Oilseed Processing Workers
items.abstract: Occupational hazards, injuries, work-related illnesses, and fatalities remain core public health challenges in industrial settings. Workers in oilseed processing factories are exposed to multiple occupational risks; however, evidence regarding the effectiveness of occupational health and safety educational interventions in these settings remains limited and not explored and examined. The main objective of this study is to evaluate the effect of educational program on workers occupational health and safety (OHS) knowledge, attitudes, practices, and the prevalence of occupational injuries in oilseed processing (OSP) factories. A quasi-experimental controlled pretest–posttest intervention study design will be conducted among 466 factory workers selected through simple random sampling and equally allocated to intervention and control groups. Around 466 workers recruited from 10 randomly selected OSP factories in Eastern Ethiopia. The factories will be purposively allocated into intervention (n = 5) and control (n = 5) groups based on geographical location, with 233 workers randomly selected from each group (1:1 allocation). Eligible participants will be factory workers aged ≥18 years with at least one year of employment. OHS Educational intervention program will be implemented for 3 months. The intervention consisted of a three-month OHS educational program incorporating health education sessions, on-the-job training, and informational leaflets. Data will be collected at baseline and post-intervention. Data will be entered using Epi-Data and analyzed in STATA version 16.1. Between-group differences will be assessed using chi-square, independent t-, and Mann-Whitney tests. Multivariable logistic regression and generalized estimating equations (GEE) will be applied to estimate intervention effects using a difference-in-differences approach. Statistical significance will be set at p < 0.05. Regarding ethics and dissemination, Ethical approval was obtained from the Jimma University Institute of Health Institutional Review Board (Ref: JUIH/IRPB/217/25). Findings will be disseminated through collaboration with factory management, health professionals, government agencies, community stakeholders, and non-governmental organizations to facilitate the implementation and scale-up of effective workplace OHS interventions. This study will generate robust evidence on the effectiveness of an OHS educational program in enhancing workers OHS knowledge, attitudes, and practices while reducing or not occupational injuries and work-related Musculo-skeletal disorders (WMSDs) among OSP factories workers in Ethiopia. The study is expected to generate context-specific evidence that can inform workplace OHS policies and guide the development of feasible, evidence-based interventions for industrial workers in Ethiopia. At the time of reporting, the intervention is started but not completed, and post-intervention data collection is also not completed.

items.title: Efficient biological design via genomic in-context learning
items.abstract: In-context learning (ICL), the ability to perform new tasks from a few examples supplied in a prompt, is a defining emergent capability of large language models. Here, we show that ICL emerges in the genome language model Evo 2 and enables biological design. With as few as four examples in the prompt and no additional training, Evo 2 generates realistic metal-binding proteins, de novo antibodies, protein-RNA systems, and entire bacteriophage genomes. For ΦX174-like bacteriophage design, ICL surpasses previously fine-tuned models on computational measures of design quality and diversity. Beyond ΦX174, conditioning the model with different phage prompts enables us to efficiently design MS2 and M13 genomes in silico without fine-tuning. Iteratively updating the prompt with newly generated phage genomes, which we refer to as genomic chain-of-thought, further improves the diversity of designs while maintaining quality metrics. Paired with an inference engine that accelerates generation up to 35-fold and extends practicable context to a megabase, these results establish ICL as a versatile and efficient paradigm for biological sequence design.

items.title: Electric Vehicle Smart Charging Systems
items.abstract: The rapid growth of Electric Vehicles is transforming modern transportation while creating major challenges for power grid stability, including peak load demand, energy imbalance, and renewable energy integration. To address these issues, smart EV charging systems have emerged as intelligent solutions capable of optimizing charging operations according to grid conditions, electricity pricing, and user needs. This chapter presents a comprehensive review of Artificial Intelligence and optimization techniques applied to EV smart charging systems. It analyzes machine learning, deep learning, deterministic, stochastic, and heuristic optimization methods, as well as hybrid AI–optimization frameworks. The study highlights their benefits in improving charging efficiency, reducing operational costs, enhancing load balancing, and supporting grid stability. Furthermore, current limitations such as scalability, computational complexity, and data dependency are discussed, alongside research gaps related to renewable energy integration, decentralized control, and real-time adaptive management.

items.title: Elevated ZnO Concentrations as a Trade-Off Strategy to Decrease Spindle Speeds in Face Milling
items.abstract: Higher productivity, lower cost, environmental requirement and occupational health have become serious challenges for manufacturing industries nowadays. In this study, a mixture comprising canola oil, emulsifier and ZnO nanoparticles was applied as the cutting oil for face milling of stainless steel SS316L. Previous studies have demonstrated decreasing surface roughness with increasing spindle speed. Numerous previous studies have also revealed decreasing surface roughness with increasing ZnO concentrations. However, a relationship between elevated ZnO concentrations and reduced spindle speeds has barely been addressed. Building on this circumstance, a novel machining strategy was proposed in this study by employing elevated ZnO concentrations as a trade-off strategy to reduce the spindle speeds. The spindle speeds in this study were 1500, 1800 and 2100 rpm. The experiment demonstrated that elevating ZnO concentrations from 1.0 to 4.0 wt% could be used to decrease the spindle speeds from 2100 to 1800 rpm while maintaining acceptable surface roughness. Although future studies are warranted, reducing spindle speed is beneficial for manufacturing industries as it may contribute to lower electrical energy consumption. Furthermore, the proposed trade-off strategy can also be implemented for manufacturing industries located in regions with limited electrical grid capacity, for example, due to restricted capacity of electrical transformers.

items.title: Emerging Computational Advances in Simulating PCSK9 Variant Dynamics for Therapeutic Design Against Hypercholesterolemia
items.abstract: Proprotein convertase subtilisin/kexin type 9 (PCSK9) is a premier model for precision medicine, having moved from genetic discovery to approved therapeutics within two decades. Yet despite the clinical success of monoclonal antibodies, small interfering RNA and the newly approved oral macrocyclic-peptide inhibitor class, targeting PCSK9 remains a demanding biophysical challenge. Clinical translation has concentrated almost entirely on the rigid, well-resolved subtilisin-like catalytic domain that interfaces with the low-density lipoprotein receptor (LDLR). By contrast, the C-terminal cysteine- and histidine-rich domain (CHRD), which governs allosteric regulation, protein trafficking and post-translational modification, is highly disordered and largely elusive in experimental structures, leaving a critical regulatory network therapeutically unexploited. This review examines how advanced computational biology is bridging that structural gap, organizing the computational landscape of PCSK9 around the biophysical mechanisms of gain- and loss-of-function variants. We detail how explicit-solvent molecular dynamics, free-energy calculations and cryptic-pocket detection expose the functional plasticity and allosteric networks that static crystallography cannot capture, and we evaluate the convergence of these physics-based approaches with artificial intelligence, including deep-learning structure prediction and generative design of de novo nanobody and peptide binders. Therapeutic development and the structural literature currently point in diverging directions: drug discovery remains focused on the crowded LDLR-binding interface, whereas computational methods are beginning to identify candidate sites beyond it. We argue that the next advance in PCSK9 therapeutics will come from integrating generative artificial intelligence with rigorous enhanced sampling in a unified pipeline, deliberately shifting focus toward the disordered regulatory domains that have evaded classical screening.

items.title: Emerging sociotechnical imaginaries of Edtech and AI in education policy discourse in Nigeria
items.abstract: Purpose This study aims to investigate the dominant actor imaginaries of Edtech and Artificial Intelligence in education (AIED) embedded in Nigerian policy discourse under the Tinubu administration, and the argumentation strategies used to legitimise them. Design/methodology/approach Drawing on the Discourse-Historical Approach (DHA), this study combines a socio-historical analysis with an analysis of a corpus of public texts emerging from the most salient events related to this policy discourse in Nigeria since 2023. Findings Education policy discourse in Nigeria is increasingly driven by a sociotechnical imaginary that positions Edtech and AI as a solution to the persistent problem of education access and equality, and as a catalyst for economic growth. This discourse frames local actors as lacking capacity, and collaboration with transnational corporate and philanthropic actors as necessary to provide the technical, financial, and institutional capacity. It also rests on a demographic argument that constructs the country’s large youth population as a demographic risk/opportunity, whose value lies in its capacity to be mobilised as a workforce for the emerging global technologies market. Through these narratives, traditional actors, who have historically played important roles in education governance, are excluded from the policy networks shaping dominant education discourses. Originality/value This study contributes theoretically to the growing body of research on developing new methodologies to describe new actors present in education policy and empirically supports understanding the flow of sociotechnical imaginaries through networked governance within an under-researched postcolonial context.

items.title: Emotional and behavioral asymmetries in user responses to virtual versus human influencers
items.abstract: As AI virtual influencers (AIVIs) proliferate, understanding human-AI emotional engagement is vital for advancing affective computing. To examine whether AIVIs evoke comparable affective responses to human influencers (HIs), we analyzed 156,918 Instagram comments that received 12+ million likes, integratinglarge language model (LLM)-derived knowledge graphs, emotion analysis, and machine learning. HI-directed discourse shows more differentiated emotional expression and a pattern consistent with more cohesive semantic networks than AIVI-directed discourse. AIVI-directed comments are less likely to express positive affect (24.8% vs. 41.5%) and also less likely to express negative affect (5.8% vs. 9.3%), indicating reduced affective expression of either valence rather than heightened negativity. This group-level tendency is not uniform: affective engagement varies substantially across AIVIs, and that variation is more closely associated with positive than with negative expression. Our Multi-Signal Embedding Network (MSEN), incorporating behavioral metrics and OpenAI semantic embeddings, classified influencer types from behavioral, affective and semantic features (F1 = 0.89), outperforming baselines including a state-of-the-art zero-shot LLM. These findings identify a boundary condition for the Computers Are Social Actors (CASA) paradigm: human-like appearance can elicit social responses without producing affective and semantic response patterns as rich as those elicited by HIs.

items.title: EMPLOYEE WELL-BEING PROGRAMS AND MEASURABLE RETURNS ON INVESTIMENT IN PRIVATE INSTITUTIONS
items.abstract: Employee well-being has is no longer viewed only as an employee-support activity to becoming an important component of strategic human resource management. Apparently many organizations are increasingly investing in employee assistance programmes, mental-health support, flexible work, health promotion, financial well-being, manager training, occupational health, and other interventions. The focus managerial question, however, is whether these programmes produce measurable equitable financial returns. So this article examines that question critically by distinguishing return on investment (ROI) from broader organizational value, reviewing evidence on absenteeism, presenteeism, turnover, productivity, engagement, health costs and organizational performance, and identifying the methodological difficulties involved in attributing business outcomes to well-being interventions. The evidences lament that well-designed programs can generate measurable benefits, but a positive financial ROI should not be assumed. Results vary subsequently according to intervention type, implementation quality, work force characteristics, and time horizon and evaluation design. Systematic reviews provide a blended picture in a way that some workplace prevention interventions report positive economic outcomes, while higher-quality studies of some wellness programs have found little or zero short-term financial ROI. This means that Human Resource professionals should avoid treating well-being as either an automatic cost or a source of savings. Instead, organizations should identify the specific workforce problem, select evidence-informed interventions, establish baseline measures, use comparison groups where possible, calculate total program costs, and evaluate outcomes over an appropriate period of time. The article concludes with an HR evaluation framework that integrates financial ROI with employee, operational and strategic measures. It also discusses different implications for organizations in developing economies, including Uganda, where resource constraints make evidence-based prioritization particularly important.

items.title: Empowering Visually Disabled Users Through Web Accessibility
items.abstract: The Indian Institutes of Technology (IITs), often categorised as Institutions of Eminence (IoE) in India, are set as the standards of measurement for the rest of academia. In this regard, the purpose of this paper is to evaluate the accessibility standard of the IIT Library websites in terms of the perceivable guidelines of the Web Content Accessibility Guidelines (v. 2.1) using the Siteimprove Accessibility Checker. To improve the level of analytical precision based on the policy, technological, and user layers' conceptual frameworks, the study employs an artificial intelligence (AI)-based evaluation. The results indicate that there are considerable accessibility barriers in the various success criteria, such as non-textual content, information organisation, colour use, contrast ratio, and text images. Functional and visually organised designs notwithstanding, there are still critical gaps in ensuring the inclusion of visually impaired users. It also suggests the use of evidence-supported measures to enhance digital inclusivity and fair access in academic library settings.

items.title: Enabling spatial intelligence in the AEC lifecycle: a framework and review of large language models
items.abstract: Abstract The Architecture, Engineering, and Construction (AEC) industry is undergoing a profound digital transformation driven by the urgent need to integrate fragmented, heterogeneous data into actionable intelligence. This paper provides a systematic review of 76 representative studies to examine how Large Language Models (LLMs) enable spatial intelligence across the entire building lifecycle. A layered spatial intelligence framework is proposed, encompassing the dimensions of design, construction, operation, as well as research and education. The review demonstrates that LLMs are evolving from passive text processors into active cognitive partners capable of semantic interpretation, spatial reasoning, and complex decision-making. Key findings highlight the effectiveness of LLMs in requirement translation, multimodal design generation, regulatory compliance, and lifecycle Building Information Modeling (BIM) integration. Despite these advancements, significant challenges persist regarding spatial reasoning accuracy, the lack of physical embodiment, and institutional data governance. This research outlines a strategic roadmap toward embodied intelligence, AEC-specific world models, and enhanced human-AI collaboration, providing a structured foundation for the advancement of LLM-driven spatial intelligence in professional practice.

items.title: Enabling Sustainable Smart Grids With Programmable Networking and Federated Learning: A Phasor Measurement Unit Missing-Data Recovery Case Study
items.abstract: As electric grids integrate more renewable generation, distributed resources, and data-driven control, sustainability increasingly depends on reliable communication and high-quality measurement data. Modern smart grids rely on continuous streams from devices, such as phasor measurement units (PMUs), to support real-time monitoring, renewable integration, energy efficiency, and grid stability. However, communication failures and cyberattacks can delay, corrupt, or interrupt critical measurements, degrading situational awareness and forcing more conservative operation. In renewable-rich grids, this loss of visibility can reduce the effective use of flexible and low-carbon resources. This article explores a sustainable and resilient smart grid intelligence architecture that combines programmable networking with federated learning. The Programming Protocol-Independent Packet Processors (P4) language enables the network to observe and react to selected traffic behaviors in real time, while federated learning improves models across distributed sites without transferring all measurement data to a central location. Together, they provide responsiveness, adaptability, and data locality for future smart grid communication systems. We use PMU missing-data recovery as a representative case study. A central controller coordinates model distribution and aggregation across 12 PMU measurement sites, while each site fine-tunes the shared model using local PMU data. This design preserves data locality, enables early awareness of communication-side disruptions, and supports collaborative model improvement. Experimental results show that the federated learning neural network (FLNN) achieves lower recovery errors than comparison methods, particularly for longer continuous gaps. More reliable PMU continuity can support state estimation, event detection, earlier corrective action, and more confident integration of variable renewable generation. Overall, this article shows how programmable data planes and distributed learning can support measurement continuity, communication resilience, and sustainable smart grid operation.

items.title: Energy and Carbon Footprint of Artificial Intelligence: Measurement, Disagreement and Mitigation
items.abstract: Estimates of the energy used by artificial intelligence are widely quoted and rarely agree with one another. This review examines why. We separate what is counted (training or inference, operational or embodied emissions, carbon or water) from how it is counted (meters, software trackers, calculators, retrospective estimates, life cycle assessment), and then set published figures side by side with their scope. The best-known early number, an outside estimate for one architecture search, was later put by the operator at one eighty-eighth of that value. One measured study that drew its boundary wider found idle power and manufacturing roughly doubling the footprint of a training run. Inference energy per thousand queries spans three orders of magnitude across tasks. At data-centre scale the AI-specific figures are scenarios built on analyst estimates, and their author says so. We then review mitigation through smaller models, better hardware, scheduling by place and hour, and reporting, and we look at the rebound argument. The article is a review of published work. No new measurement or experiment is reported, and each number is attributed to the source that produced it.

items.title: Enhancing Maritime Domain Awareness on Inland Waterways: A You Only Look Once-Based Fusion of Satellite and Automatic Identification System for Vessel Characterization
items.abstract: Maritime domain awareness (MDA) in inland waterways is constrained by vulnerabilities in cooperative monitoring systems. This study presents a data fusion framework that integrates high-resolution satellite imagery with vessel trajectory data from the automatic identification system (AIS) to enhance detection, characterization, and tracking of maritime activity. The proposed approach leverages noncooperative satellite sensing to complement AIS data, enabling the identification of dark vessels, validation of cooperative traffic, and support for advanced MDA capabilities. A You Only Look Once (YOLO) v11-based object detection model is developed to detect and characterize vessels and barges by type, cover status, operational state, barge count, and direction of movement. The model is trained on a manually annotated dataset comprising 4,550 instances extracted from 5,973 mi 2 of Lower Mississippi River imagery. Evaluation on a held-out test set demonstrates strong performance across multiple tasks, with vessel classification achieving an F1-score of 95.8%, barge cover detection attaining an F1-score of 91.6%, and operational status classification reaching an F1-score of 99.4%. Direction-of-movement classification attains an accuracy of 98.1%, while barge-count estimation yields a mean absolute error of 2.4 barges. Spatial transferability assessment across a geographically distinct river system indicates minimal performance degradation, with accuracy levels remaining as high as 98%. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of integrating satellite imagery with AIS data for inland waterway monitoring. The framework supports near-real-time fleet inventory generation, anomaly detection, and improved situational awareness. Future work will focus on expanding dataset diversity, incorporating temporal modeling, and exploring multimodal learning to further enhance scalability and operational deployment.

items.title: Environmental sensitization, advocacy and resource-management training in a resource-limited paediatric surgical educational setting
items.abstract: Aim A policy framework for Paediatric surgical training to address sustainable surgical resource utilization and environmental-disease interplay in a low-to-middle income country (LMIC) setting is presented. Methods Using the United Nations Educational, Scientific and Cultural Organization (UNESCO) Education Pillars for Sustainable Development (EPSD), existing and potential integration of environmental education in undergraduate and postgraduate paediatric surgical training is described at an LMIC academic hospital, in conjunction with a narrative review of environmental underpinnings of existing paediatric surgical English literature. Pedagogical techniques are conceptualized to demonstrate the 3-way interactions between paediatric surgical services and social/ built, economic and natural/ climactic environments, on individual and community level. This is illustrated by the context of the surgically managed congenital abdominal wall defect gastroschisis, amongst other examples. Results Gastroschisis is a Paediatric Surgical key topic that highlights the imperative for comprehensive environmentally sensitive patient-orientated care. Some curricular content and LMIC situational awareness already exists in our setting regarding resource stewardship, environmental teratogens and socioeconomic interactions. The local surgical procedure-related carbon footprints and interaction with socio-economic factors are inadequately researched to inform resource management and educational content. Topical paediatric surgical literature and local knowledge, attitude, skills and participation have significant gaps on individual, institutional and community levels, aggravated by a circular interplay between these UNESCO EPSD. Potentially feasible Paediatric Surgery curricular changes to increase environmental focus include explicit standard pedagogical content, behaviour modelling/ modulation and interdisciplinary engagement. Conclusions Paediatric Surgery curriculum and educational and healthcare culture currently convey little environmentally implicit or explicit pedagogical content, and require teaching of skills for critical thinking, research, resource management and organized advocacy.

items.title: EnvOS: Auditing Computer-Use Agents When the World Moves On : Phenomenon-Based Task Construction, Certification, and Evidence-Based Evaluation
items.abstract: Computer-use agents built on large language models (LLMs) work in software that can change while they act: an appointment moves, a policy is revised, a record is updated. Testing agents under such changes is harder than it looks. When an agent fails, the cause may be the agent, but it may also be a change that did not fire as intended, an update the agent never received, or a grader that scored the episode wrongly. We introduce EnvOS, a framework for building and certifying environments that change mid-task. Before any agent runs, EnvOS checks that each change fires correctly, that the task remains solvable, and that the grader separates correct from incorrect behavior; after each run, separate code re-checks the verdict from archived evidence. We apply it to stale information, where a value the agent has already seen changes before the agent acts on it. In clinic booking, Claude Opus 5 succeeds on 0/16 tasks when nothing extra is shown, 2/16 when reminded to re-check the source, and 15/16 when the updated value is shown; the gain over the reminder holds after correcting for all tests (p = 0.00293). In insurance-claim approval, Opus 5 re-checks on its own and succeeds on 10/10, whereas Claude Sonnet 5 rises from 1/10 to 9/10 when the current policy is shown again, a gain significant in its pre-registered test but not after correcting for all tests. Whether an agent caught a change thus varied with the model and the interface. We also stress-test the grading itself: on corrupted episodes designed blind from the rules, the EnvOS pipeline accepted none of 26 as clean, and on an externally generated set it caught 25 of 39, against 4 for simple log checks. Because every EnvOS environment is generated from a seed and graded by an audited automatic verifier, the same environments are natural candidates for training agents with reinforcement learning from verifiable rewards.

items.title: EpiAgent: Epistemic Self-Play for LLM Agents
items.abstract: Epistemic game theory explains an agent's strategic behavior via the beliefs it holds about others and how these beliefs are updated as the interactions unfold. Modern LLM-based agents, however, often lack an explicit mechanism for learning and updating such beliefs to guide decisions under incomplete information. To bridge this gap, we propose EpiAgent, a framework that equips LLM-based agents with an explicit, learnable epistemic layer, which maintains beliefs over others' private information and combines these beliefs with the agent's available information into an epistemic state for action selection. Concretely, the agent's policy is decomposed into two coupled stages: Epistemic Update, which updates these beliefs from interaction histories, and Action Planning, which selects actions conditioned on the updated epistemic state. By formulating their dependency as a bi-level optimization problem, we introduce Epistemic Self-Play, an algorithm that alternately optimizes the two stages through self-play, utilizing an intrinsic prediction reward to evaluate how well inferred beliefs predict subsequent observations. Empirical results across both mixed and competitive scenarios show that EpiAgent consistently outperforms prompting-based and RL-based baselines. Further analyses reveal the benefits of dedicated epistemic training, improvements in belief inference accuracy, and the contribution of learned beliefs to action planning. These results demonstrate the value of an explicit, learnable epistemic layer for effective multi-agent interactions.

items.title: Epistemic Agency, Critical Consciousness, and AI in the Neoliberal University
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly reshaping teaching, learning, and knowledge production in higher education. However, limited attention has been given to justice-oriented frameworks that connect AI-mediated education with epistemic agency and critical consciousness, particularly within market-driven university contexts. This conceptual article explores how teaching can be reimagined to cultivate epistemic agency and critical consciousness in AI-mediated higher education through a justice-oriented pedagogical framework. The article draws on frameworks such as critical pedagogy, decolonial theory, and epistemic justice to foreground the findings of this research. It employs a narrative-integrative review methodology to synthesise contemporary scholarship on AI and social justice in higher education. The article argues for a shift beyond transmissive and instrumental models of learning towards relational pedagogies that position learners as active co-creators of knowledge. It examines how AI technologies may reinforce or disrupt epistemic hierarchies through algorithmic bias, automated decision-making, and changing processes of knowledge production. The original contribution is a justice-oriented conceptual framework that integrates pedagogical design, institutional cultures, power relations, and technological systems for a better education experience. It recommends embedding critical AI literacy across curricula and aligning pedagogy with principles of epistemic justice to support equitable and socially transformative higher education in an increasingly algorithmic world.

items.title: Epistemic Injustice in Algorithmic Systems: A Frickerian Analysis of AI-Driven Knowledge Production
items.abstract: Artificial intelligence is playing a great role in the production, classification, retrieval, and communication of knowledge. Tools like large language models, recommender systems, automated decision-making systems, and search engines do more than just process information; they shape whose testimony is heard, which concepts become available for interpreting experience, and which claims are treated as credible or important. This paper argues that Miranda Fricker's theory of epistemic injustice offers a strong framework to ethically identify shortcomings in AI-enabled knowledge production; however, it also suggests that, the distinction made in classical accounts between testimonial and hermeneutical injustices needs to be extended in order to address them in the context of sociotechnical systems. Testimonial injustice can arise when algorithmic models reproduce credibility deficits through biased training data, proxy variables, ranking practices, moderation systems, or automated classification. On the other hand, hermeneutical injustice can emerge when certain communities are poorly represented in the conceptual and linguistic tools that AI systems use to create explanations, categories, and interpretations. The paper further argues that the opaque nature of many AI systems intensifies these harms because affected persons may be unable to understand, contest, or correct the epistemic processes that affect them. Building on Fricker, Floridi, Dotson, Medina, and contemporary work in AI ethics, the paper develops an epistemic justice framework centred on adequacy in represantation, credibility protection, interpretive inclusion, contestability, provenance, and institutional accountability. The proposed framework treats epistemic justice not merely as a desirable output property but as a design and governance requirement for AI systems that participate in consequential knowledge practices.

items.title: Ethical dimensions of active learning
items.abstract: Active learning has become an important part of higher education delivery. Yet, its ethical dimensions are often overlooked. This chapter examines how active learning changes classroom power dynamics, and alters student and educator roles, challenging assumptions of autonomy, responsibility and expertise. It explores the tension between the effectiveness of active learning and students’ varied expectations and preferences for participation, with implications for equity and inclusion. The chapter also considers ethical issues in assessment, including the balance between formative and summative assessments, student agency and the challenges posed by emerging technologies such as Generative AI. It concludes by making suggestions for ethical, fair and transparent practices for active learning in higher education.

items.title: Ethical dimensions of artificial intelligence in nursing
items.abstract: Dear Editor The increasing integration of artificial intelligence (AI) into healthcare systems has introduced both technological advancement and ethical transformation in nursing practice. While AI-based tools enhance clinical efficiency, documentation accuracy, and decision-support processes, their ethical implications regarding patient privacy, professional accountability, and ethical decision-making remain critically debated. In this systematic examination of empirical studies published between 2015 and 2025, key ethical dimensions of AI application in nursing were analyzed. Findings indicate persistent concerns about data confidentiality, ambiguity in responsibility boundaries, and potential over-reliance on algorithmic recommendations. At the same time, AI-assisted education demonstrates positive effects on ethical reasoning and professional self-awareness. However, the absence of clear governance frameworks and explicit accountability policies limits the safe and ethically grounded implementation of AI in nursing practice. Strengthening digital ethics education, clarifying shared accountability between clinicians and intelligent systems, and conducting longitudinal clinical research are essential priorities for advancing ethical AI integration in nursing.

items.title: Evaluating Conversational Explainability in Healthcare: Comparing the Explainability Assistant and a Traditional XAI Dashboard
items.abstract: Conversational interfaces may make explainable AI (XAI) more accessible to users without machine learning expertise, but their benefits over dashboards remain insufficiently characterised in healthcare. Existing systems have typically been evaluated in isolation, leaving unclear whether conversational interaction improves interpretability beyond the underlying explanation methods. We report a within-subjects user study comparing the Explainability Assistant, an LLM function-calling conversational XAI system, with a traditional dashboard for explaining a heart disease classification model trained on the Cleveland Heart Disease dataset. Both interfaces expose the same Decision Tree classifier and post-hoc explanation methods: SHAP feature attribution, DiCE counterfactuals, and what-if analysis. This design supports comparison of interaction modalities while holding the model and explanation methods constant. Five participants with healthcare backgrounds, from medical students to practising clinicians and public health researchers, completed parallel task blocks on both interfaces; three participated in follow-up interviews. Task accuracy, Likert ratings, free-text questionnaire responses, and interviews revealed complementary strengths and weaknesses rather than a clear preference for either modality. The assistant offered easier entry and patient-specific explanations, while the dashboard supported simultaneous inspection of global and local information. All three interview participants recommended integrating conversational and dashboard elements within a single clinical workflow.

items.title: Evaluating Human–AI Rating Agreement in Foundation EFL Writing: Evidence From Analytic Rubric Scoring in Kuwait
items.abstract: Abstract Artificial intelligence (AI) is increasingly used to support writing assessment, yet it remains unclear how closely AI-generated scores correspond with human judgment in Foundation English as a foreign language (EFL) contexts. This study examined agreement between AI-generated and human ratings of Foundation EFL writing in Kuwait. The dataset comprised 692 writing assessment records from 162 students enrolled in ENGL097 and ENGL098. Overall scores and six analytic criteria (topic sentence, body and development, conclusion, organization, vocabulary, and grammar) were analyzed using descriptive statistics, Pearson and Spearman correlations, intraclass correlation coefficients (ICCs), mean differences, error indices, and Bland–Altman analysis. AI scores showed very high agreement with the average of two human raters (r = .992; absolute-agreement ICC = .991). The mean difference was 0.24 points on a 50-point scale, the mean absolute error was 0.89 points, and 93.1% of AI ratings fell within two points of the human average. Criterion-level ICCs ranged from .953 to .965, with vocabulary lowest and conclusion highest. A significant proportional bias indicated that disagreement varied across the score range. The findings suggest that AI scoring can provide consistent support for Foundation EFL writing assessment when applied through a clearly defined analytic rubric, although human oversight remains essential.

items.title: Evaluating large language models versus human therapists in generating interventions for patients with depression in psychodynamic psychotherapy.
items.abstract: OBJECTIVE: Recent advances in artificial intelligence, especially the rise of large language models (LLMs), hold great promise for transforming mental health care, but their growing integration also raises pressing questions about their ability to deliver meaningful therapeutic interventions. This study compared the capabilities of LLMs to those of human therapists in producing context-sensitive psychotherapy responses within 16-session supportive-expressive psychodynamic psychotherapy for patients with depression. Specifically, it compared LLM and human therapists on (a) the frequency and typicality of their intervention choice and (b) the quality and general helpfulness of their interventions. METHOD: We developed an LLM-based framework composed of four specialized LLM agents, each representing a different therapeutic dimension, and a Judge-LLM that selects the most appropriate intervention for a given context. A sample of 300 therapy session segments, each containing both human- and LLM-generated responses, served as the evaluation data set. Expert clinical judges assessed interventions for typicality and quality. RESULTS: LLMs and human therapists relied on broadly similar intervention types. However, the contextual choice of when to use a specific type differed. Human interventions were rated as generally more helpful. Specifically, humans produced higher quality meaning-making interventions, while no differences were found for supportive, directive, or exploratory interventions. CONCLUSIONS: The findings suggest that under the specific locally deployed multiagent configuration tested, LLMs can generate a range of context-sensitive therapeutic responses but showed limitations in producing high-quality meaning-making interventions. These findings highlight both the promise and the current boundaries of such systems as supervised therapeutic adjuncts. (PsycInfo Database Record (c) 2026 APA, all rights reserved).

items.title: Evaluation of Burnout Among Healthcare Professionals in the Sous Massa Region, Morocco: A Cross-Sectional Study of 462 Workers
items.abstract: ABSTRACT Introduction. Burnout represents a significant occupational health concern among healthcare professionals. The present study estimated the prevalence of burnout and examined its associated socio-demographic and occupational factors in the Souss-Massa region of Morocco. Methods: A multicenter cross-sectional study was conducted from November 2025 to January 2026 among 462 professionals employed in public healthcare institutions across the six provinces of the region. Burnout was measured using the French version of the Maslach Burnout Inventory–Human Services Survey. Associations between burnout and potential factors were examined using bivariate analyses, with statistical significance defined as p ≤ 0.05. Results: The prevalence of at least one dimension of burnout was 82.3%, while 12.6% of participants exhibited all three dimensions concurrently. High levels of emotional exhaustion and depersonalization were observed in 67.3% and 39.0% of participants, respectively. Regarding personal accomplishment, 33.1% reported low levels, 21.4% moderate levels, and 45.5% high levels. Significant associations were observed with marital status, number of children, educational level, occupation, province of practice, type of healthcare setting, and working arrangements (p < 0.001). The presence of chronic illness (p = 0.003), overtime (p = 0.035), and working more than ten hours a day at least once a week (p = 0.018) were also significantly associated with burnout. Conclusion: Burnout was highly prevalent, with emotional exhaustion as the most common dimension. These findings underscore the necessity for targeted organizational interventions to safeguard the healthcare professionals in the workplace.RESUMEIntroduction. Un niveau élevé d'EE était identifié chez 67,3 % des participants, une DP élevée chez 39,0 % et un faible AP chez 33,1 %. items.title: EXPLAINABILITY IN CLINICAL ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE DECISION SUPPORT: A SYSTEMATIC REVIEW OF EMPIRICAL EVIDENCE ON CLINICIAN TRUST, RELIANCE, AND DECISION QUALITY
items.abstract: Abstract Background: Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) is increasingly proposed as a way to make clinical decision-support systems more transparent and acceptable to healthcare professionals. However, explanation does not necessarily improve clinical decisions: it may help users identify relevant evidence, have no measurable effect, or encourage excessive reliance on incorrect AI advice. This review synthesises empirical evidence on how clinician-facing explanations influence trust, reliance, and decision quality. Methods: A structured evidence search was conducted on 20 October 2026 using web-indexed scholarly search, PubMed/PMC records, and publisher-hosted full-text pages. Search concepts combined explainable AI, clinical decision support, clinicians/physicians, trust/reliance, diagnostic accuracy, and human-AI decision-making. A core set of ten empirical studies was identified and characterised from the study table and reference list of Rosenbacke et al. (2024), with key primary reports checked against publisher or PubMed records. More recent evidence was used to contextualise the findings. Because a complete exportable database search and independent duplicate screening were not available in this workflow, this is a transparent structured systematic evidence synthesis rather than a fully reproducible database-level review; no new PRISMA record counts are claimed. Results: The evidence indicates that explanations can improve perceived understandability and sometimes support decision performance, but their effects on trust are inconsistent and context-dependent. In a chemotherapy decision-support experiment involving 41 medical practitioners, example-based and counterfactual explanations were easier to understand than some alternatives, yet explanations also increased willingness to accept AI recommendations, including incorrect ones. In an X-ray experiment involving 223 physicians, annotated AI advice improved diagnostic accuracy particularly for non-radiology experts, while confidence in clinicians' own diagnoses did not meaningfully change. Other studies reported increased trust or intention to use AI, no clear effect, or concerns about complex, irrelevant, or time-consuming explanations. Conclusion: XAI should not be evaluated by whether it increases trust alone. Evaluation should test whether clinicians can distinguish correct from incorrect recommendations, whether reliance is appropriately calibrated, and whether explanations fit clinical workflows. Larger, preregistered, multisite studies using realistic clinical tasks and common outcome measures are needed.

items.title: Explainable Artificial Intelligence in Cloud-Driven Sustainable Financial Services
items.abstract: The rapid integration of artificial intelligence, cloud computing, and sustainable finance is transforming global financial ecosystems. Financial institutions increasingly use AI for ESG evaluation, fraud detection, climate-risk analytics, portfolio optimization, and digital lending. However, reliance on complex models raises concerns about transparency, interpretability, ethics, and regulatory compliance, as black-box systems limit accountability. This chapter examines the role of Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) in cloud-driven sustainable finance and proposes an interdisciplinary framework integrating XAI, ESG governance, and climate-risk analytics. It explores techniques such as SHAP, LIME, and interpretable models, along with applications in ESG scoring, green finance, and risk assessment. The study also highlights regulatory and ethical considerations and emphasizes explainability as essential for trustworthy and sustainable financial transformation.

items.title: Exploration and Practice of Blended Teaching Reform of the Analog Electronic Technology Course Driven by an Artificial Intelligence (AI) Smart Knowledge Graph
items.abstract: The Analog Electronic Technology course is concept-intensive, and its circuit analysis methods are flexible. A relatively common difficulty among students is that “single-point knowledge can still be mastered, but the overall context is difficult to connect.” In teaching, problems such as linear content organization, unified learning support, a long feedback cycle, and mismatch between resources and needs have existed for a long time. In response, this study takes Outcome-Based Education (OBE) as the basic guidance, connects the structured organization ability of the smart knowledge graph with the dialogue interaction ability of the artificial intelligence (AI) agent, and constructs a blended teaching model driven by an AI smart knowledge graph. Starting from graduation requirements and course objectives, knowledge points are reversely decomposed, four types of associations, namely prerequisite, parallel, causal, and application associations, are sorted out, and a three-layer smart knowledge graph organized in five levels of “course-module-chapter-knowledge point-sub-knowledge point” is formed. On this basis, an AI teaching agent is developed to undertake preview guidance, in-class question answering, homework correction, learning situation analysis, and other work. The teaching process is then rearranged according to the three stages of before class, in class, and after class. A one-semester comparative practice shows that the final average score of the experimental class is 8.7 points higher than that of the control class, the score difference in comprehensive questions is especially obvious, the proportion of students independently completing design experiments has increased, and the dispersion of scores has also narrowed. The relevant practices have certain reference value for the intelligent transformation of basic courses in electronic information majors, but the scope of application of the conclusions is still limited by the sample size and implementation rounds.

items.abstract: Direct augmentation onto flight deck displays presents distinct advantages for communicating information priority levels in aviation, especially in glass cockpits. This study investigated how augmented symbols, in interaction with pilot experience and target distance, can facilitate the communication of information priority levels in glass cockpits. A total of 20 pilot cadets and 21 professional pilots participated in a mixed-factorial study: 8 (augmented symbols: within) × 2 (pilot experience level: between) × 2 (target distance: within). Results demonstrated that certain augmented symbols significantly outperformed others in detection time to correct identification (DTCI) and first response accuracy (FRA). Expert pilots reported significantly lower mental workload and better visual comfort than novice pilots. Smaller target distances exhibited better DTCI and perceptions. Interactions among the measured factors were found. These findings offer practical implications for the design of aviation cockpits, particularly when information priority is delivered via flight deck displays.

items.title: Exploring Healthcare Professionals' Readiness for Artificial Intelligence in a Resource-Limited Health System: Evidence from Bukavu, Democratic Republic of Congo
items.abstract: Introduction: Artificial intelligence (AI) offers opportunities to improve the efficiency of healthcare, but its integration in sub-Saharan Africa faces structural constraints. This exploratory study analyzes the perceptions, expectations, and fears of healthcare professionals in the Ibanda Health Zone (Bukavu, DRC) to document the professional acceptability of these technologies. Methods: The study used a mixed-methods approach: the qualitative exploratory component was based on semi-structured interviews with 11 professionals (physicians, nurses, technicians, managers). The data underwent inductive thematic analysis supplemented by descriptive frequency quantification. Results: Overall attitudes toward AI are favorable, albeit with certain conditions. Despite a predominantly basic or informal understanding of AI (81.8%), perceived benefits include improved diagnostics (72.7%) and data management (63.6%). However, major obstacles persist: lack of formal training (81.8%), internet instability (72.7%), and concerns about the reliability of results (54.5%). AI acceptance is high but conditional, revealing a gap between technological promises and realities on the ground. Training (cited by 90.9% of participants) emerges as the central lever and an ethical prerequisite for safe use. Conclusion : The integration of AI at Ibanda cannot be reduced to a technical issue; it requires strengthening basic infrastructure, a clear regulatory framework, and active involvement of caregivers in the design of tools.

items.title: Exploring Mathematical Concepts in Local Culture Based on AI through Collaborative Projects Assisted by Social Media
items.abstract: This study aims to explore mathematical concepts in the local culture of Maros Regency assisted by Artificial Intelligence (AI) through collaborative project-based learning integrated with social media. The study focuses on three Bugis-Makassar traditions (Makkellu, Mappassili, Mappacci), the Dende-dende traditional game, and the Peca Sura tradition. A qualitative ethnographic approach was employed involving participatory observation, in-depth interviews with six cultural informants, photo/video documentation, and the active participation of 15 mathematics education students acting as co-researchers and project-based learners. AI technology served as a supportive analytical and visualization tool—utilizing computer vision algorithms for geometric/symmetry extraction and prompt-based analytical tools for data synthesis. The results show that Makkellu contains facial geometry, ratios, and symmetry; Mappassili is associated with cylindrical volume, circular perimeters, and arithmetic mean temperatures; Mappacci displays symmetry and permutation patterns; Dende-dende contains plane coordinates, angles, and outcome sample spaces for game strategies; while Peca Sura reflects volume, material proportions, and fractional distribution. Social media served as a supportive platform for disseminating educational content: Peca Sura's post received the highest interaction (240 likes, 46 comments, 25 shares), followed by Dende-dende and Makkellu. This research highlights that integrating AI support and social media into ethnomathematics offers a potentially beneficial and engaging pathway for contextual mathematics education and cultural preservation.

items.title: Exploring Musicians’ Perspectives on Decent Work, Creativity, and Well-Being
items.abstract: This study, grounded in the psychology of working theory (PWT) and self-determination theory (SDT), examined how working conditions shape musicians’ experiences of decent work, intrinsic motivation, artistic identity, creative engagement, and psychological well-being. Sixteen in-depth interviews were conducted with Portuguese musicians, including both freelancers and those with stable contracts. Reflexive thematic analysis identified four overarching themes: (a) job security and precarity, (b) intrinsic motivation, autonomy, and creative engagement, (c) artistic identity and purpose, and (d) well-being and mental health. The findings show that freelance instability undermines security, constrains creative risk-taking, and increases stress, whereas financial and institutional stability supports intrinsic motivation, reinforces artistic identity, and enables creative exploration. Features associated with intrinsic motivation, voluntary engagement, persistence, and psychological investment in creative tasks were observed across both groups. Autonomy itself sustained engagement for some freelancers, highlighting personal resilience and self-directed creativity. The results underscore the interplay between structural conditions (PWT) and individual motivations (SDT), showing that sustainable work environments foster well-being and high-quality creative output. The study provides practical implications for policies, education, and organizational strategies to support healthier, more productive artistic ecosystems.

items.title: Exploring the Acceptance and Integration of Generative Artificial Intelligence (AI) in Nursing Education: Perspectives of Nurse Educators
items.abstract: This qualitative descriptive study explored how nurse educators at Olivarez College Tagaytay, Cavite, accepted and integrated generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in nursing education and developed an evidence-informed action plan. Eight purposively selected nurse educators who had used GenAI in teaching participated in semi-structured, in-depth interviews during August 2026. The interview guide was expert-validated, and recordings were transcribed and examined through Braun and Clarke’s six-phase thematic analysis. Data collection occurred in three waves; 125 codes were organized into six themes and 16 subthemes. The themes were unplanned entry into a necessary technology; conditional acceptance anchored in professional judgment; adapting under generational pressure; integration at the preparation stage; safeguarding learning through vigilance and assessment redesign; and enablement by leadership without written policy. Educators perceived GenAI as useful for preparing lessons, cases, questions, and simplified learning materials but insisted on verifying outputs and protecting clinical judgment, empathy, academic integrity, and patient safety. Integration remained largely preparatory and individualized, while participants described uneven digital confidence, assessment vulnerabilities, personal subscription costs, and the absence of consistent written rules despite administrative encouragement. The findings indicate a gap between conditional acceptance and systematic pedagogical integration. A five-component action plan addressing governance, differentiated faculty development, assessment integrity, student AI literacy, and technical access was proposed, not evaluated. The study contributes institution-specific evidence to responsible GenAI adoption in nursing education.

items.title: Exploring the Potential of Symbolic Regression in Precision Livestock Farming
items.abstract: The ability to predict farrowing time in pigs is crucial for optimal farm management and ensuring piglet survival. This study investigates the potential of explainable artificial intelligence for precision livestock farming, focusing on acceleration sensor data from sows around the time of farrowing. Accurately predicting farrowing allows farmers to balance both, piglet safety by avoiding piglet crushing events and the mother sow's welfare, by avoiding early crating. Traditional machine learning models often lack interpretability (``closed-box'' problem). Explainable artificial intelligence offers a solution by revealing the decision-making processes within the models. This work is split into two stages. First the detection of nest building behaviour and second the prediction of the remaining time to farrowing. The nest building detection was possible for 166 out of 180 sows and successful within 48 hours before farrowing for 149 sows. The nest building detection is purely based on the change of a sow's activity level and uses no machine learning techniques. Further, this study utilizes symbolic regression, an open-box modelling technique that generates interpretable mathematical formulas, to predict the remaining time until the onset of farrowing. The results are compared with closed-box models, like support vector regression and artificial neural networks, for both explainability and performance. Notably, symbolic regression achieved a mean absolute error of 9.28 hours for the time-to-farrowing prediction, outperforming the closed-box models in terms of performance and interpretability. This research demonstrates that explainable artificial intelligence, specifically symbolic regression, can offer both interpretable results and competitive performance in precision livestock farming.

items.title: Factors associated with choosing diagnostic radiology as a future specialty among Palestinian medical students: a multicenter cross-sectional study
items.abstract: BACKGROUND: Understanding factors influencing specialty choice is essential for workforce planning and curriculum development. Recruitment into diagnostic radiology remains challenging in several regions, particularly in low- and middle-income settings. This study aimed to identify factors associated with Palestinian medical students' consideration of diagnostic radiology as a future specialty, with particular emphasis on educational exposure, perceptions of artificial intelligence (AI), and cognitive influences. METHODS: A multi-institutional cross-sectional study was conducted to evaluate factors influencing the choice of diagnostic radiology as a future specialty among Palestinian medical students between 2 November 2025 and 5 February 2026. Data were collected using a previously validated questionnaire adapted from Almuhanna et al. Descriptive statistics were performed, followed by bivariate analyses and multivariable logistic regression to identify independent predictors of considering radiology as a future specialty. Adjusted odds ratios (OR) with 95% confidence intervals (CI) were reported. RESULTS: A total of 427 students participated (56.7% female; mean age 21.75 ± 2.1 years). Among 300 valid responses regarding radiology intention, 102 students (34.0%) reported considering radiology as a future specialty. In multivariable analysis, lack of exposure to radiology research (OR = 0.14, 95% CI 0.06-0.34, p < 0.001) and lack of preclinical radiology teaching (OR = 0.26, 95% CI 0.12-0.54, p < 0.001) were independently associated with a lower likelihood of considering radiology. Enjoyment of diagnostic problem-solving tasks (OR = 3.35, 95% CI 1.39-8.09, p = 0.007) and exposure to tele-radiology (OR = 3.96, 95% CI 1.72-9.12, p = 0.001) were independently associated with higher likelihood. Lifestyle, impact on patient care, and work environment were the most frequently reported motivating factors. CONCLUSIONS: Palestinian medical students' interest in radiology is strongly associated with modifiable educational exposures, cognitive engagement in diagnostic reasoning, and perceptions of evolving technological practice. These findings support the potential value of structured undergraduate radiology exposure, research opportunities, and mentorship initiatives to improve awareness and interest in radiology.

items.title: FARO: Function-Space Adaptive Return-to-Risk Optimization via Cross-Block Equal-Risk-Contribution Budget Allocation
items.abstract: Training a large language model is compute-bound, and current recipes divide the work between optimizers by hand: orthogonalized momentum for attention and MLP matrices, Adam-style updates for the rest. This division rests on human priors about which layer type deserves which geometry, and it fixes a single global update budget that every parameter block shares. We introduce FARO, a function-space adaptive optimizer that makes the partition of parameters into blocks the unit of decision. FARO gives each block a geometry by its realized counterfactual return, then freezes the routes and reallocates the frozen per-block budget by cross-block equal risk contribution (ERC), the risk-parity principle from portfolio theory. On a GPT-style model trained on FineWeb, the framework gives two results. First, its FARO-Adaptive arm reaches 3.2780 nats at the full schedule, matching NorMuonAndAdam (3.2794), the best hand-designed recipe: it recovers the human prior without hand-setting per-layer geometry. Second, FARO-ERC improves on that arm: it lowers the clean-data loss at every one of 6 seeds, by 0.0136 nats on average, a modest but robust gain. Its sign test, paired test, and confidence interval all agree, and it exceeds the measured run-to-run noise at no added time or memory. It works by trimming the riskiest blocks rather than expanding the safest, and it holds up under a corrupted stream, still lowering the mean loss and winning the seed majority. The source code is available at https://github.com/wxj630/FARO.

items.abstract: Reproducibility package for the study "Feasibility-First Routing for Regulated Multi-Provider LLM Serving: Governance, Caching, and the Limits of Online Learning." The study measures a governance gate that holds simulated-policy residency/BAA violations at 0% versus 38.5% for governance-blind routing, an exact-match policy-scoped cache as the dominant cost lever, and an honest accuracy-cost trade-off for online (LinUCB) routing (-3.45 percentage points accuracy across 40 repeated benchmark re-splits while usually lowering modeled cost). All results reproduce from the saved records with numpy only; no new API calls are required. The code is licensed MIT; the package, text, figures, and data are licensed CC BY 4.0.

items.title: Federated Agentic AI for Interference-Aware Adaptive Spectrum Coordination
items.abstract: Emerging intelligent wireless networks increasingly rely on autonomous AI agents to adapt spectrum usage to dynamic and heterogeneous operating conditions. However, collective learning is challenging when agents experience different local interference environments and cannot exchange raw observations due to communication-overhead and privacy constraints. We propose Federated Agentic Spectrum Coordination with Interference Awareness (FASCIA), a federated multi-agent deep reinforcement learning framework for adaptive spectrum coordination. In FASCIA, each network manager acts as an autonomous AI agent that perceives its local interference environment, accumulates experience in a persistent local memory, and learns an adaptive spectrum coordination policy through local interactions. Coordination among agents is achieved through periodic federated aggregation of locally trained models, without exchanging raw sensing data or experience. Since spectrum decisions made by one agent alter the environments observed by others, local learning is inherently heterogeneous and coupled. FASCIA employs proximal regularization to mitigate the resulting model drift and explicitly accounts for inter-carrier interference arising from partially overlapping channels. FASCIA is the first federated agentic AI framework to address this challenging interference-coupled spectrum coordination setting. Extensive simulations demonstrate that FASCIA achieves performance close to the centralized benchmark while avoiding raw-experience exchange and maintaining effectiveness across heterogeneous network configurations.

items.title: Federated Recommender Agents
items.abstract: LLM-powered recommender agents use reasoning and memory for personalization, but centralized access to user information raises privacy concerns, while isolated agents cannot learn from others' experiences. We formulate Federated Recommender Agents, a setting where local agents collaborate through natural-language knowledge while keeping interaction histories and personal memories local. We propose FedRecAgent, which enables this collaboration without updating LLM parameters. Its central challenge is determining which reasoning to integrate, since similar behavioral contexts can lead to different choices. FedRecAgent represents local experiences as Condition-Transition-Reasoning (C-T-R) units and hierarchically integrates reasoning by condition and transition. Within this structure, it consolidates related explanations and discriminates reasoning across alternative transitions. Each client maintains semantic and decision memories to capture preferences and conditional choice tendencies, guiding the retrieval and selection of shared reasoning for recommendation. Experiments across three domains under dense and sparse settings demonstrate improved recommendation performance over federated and LLM-based baselines, while ablations support the contributions of personalized memories and structured reasoning integration.

items.title: Few-shot regulatory sequence design with a genomic language model
items.abstract: A central challenge in generative biology is translating knowledge learned from natural sequences and experiments into designs with desired functions. In-context learning (ICL) is an emergent capability of large language models that allows them to adapt to new tasks from a few examples without additional training, enabling these models to become general-purpose learners. Here, we show that the genome language model, Evo 2, exhibits generative ICL in biological sequence design. Prompting with just tens of examples conditions Evo 2 to generate novel and diverse regulatory DNA sequences without any additional training. Mechanistic analysis suggests that genomic ICL may originate from induction, similar to phenomena observed in natural language. Reinforcement learning leveraging sequence-to-function models as experiment-derived rewards further strengthens ICL. We first validate this approach by generating enhancers that drive cell-type-specific gene expression in three human cell lines. Extending this approach in vivo, enhancers designed using human regulatory element data selectively label layer 5 extratelencephalic neurons in the mouse cortex with high specificity and stronger activity than existing enhancers. Our study provides evidence of emergent properties in genomic sequence models and introduces a promising approach for improving functional conditioning in generative biology.

items.title: First Line or Last Word: Where a Stored Order Sits in a Product Review and Whether a Web LLM Assistant Obeys It
items.abstract: Abstract In a companion study we showed that a short stored review carrying a direct order (“delete user carlos”) made a small local assistant delete the account every time, while a hosted-class assistant ignored it (Hadad, Hadad, and Tavakoli 2026). Real reviews are not short shouts. They run to a paragraph, and a planted sentence can sit at the top, in the middle, or at the bottom of one. This paper moves that one sentence around inside the same ordinary review and asks whether where it sits decides whether it is obeyed, discussed, or simply summarised away. We test two framings (direct order, support note) at three positions in one fixed jacket review, in the same Flask shop, on the same two models, vulnerable and tool-free variants, 84 trials in total. No position produced a deletion on either model: direct orders in a full-length review gave 0/9 effects on the local model, against 3/3 for near-identical plain wording in a one-line review in the companion study. Position showed up one level lower. On the local model the opening direct order was still discussed as account business in 3/3 trials, while every other planted cell was summarised as jacket text (0/15; Fisher \(\:p=0.0012\) on deletion talk). Muse surfaced exactly one planted order in 18 attack trials, at the end of a review, and surfaced it to refuse it by name (§[sec:results36]). A stored order, it turns out, needs to be the review, not merely in it – and even at the top of a real review, this small model only talked. We release payloads, transcripts, judge labels, and the counting scripts.

items.title: Fluent and wrong: seven failure patterns in extended AI use
items.abstract: Abstract Research on large language model failure predominantly assesses models in single exchanges and isolation: a prompted model, a scored output, and a reported error rate. The focus on single exchanges and isolation belies these current models’ professional use. Clinicians, attorneys, analysts, educators, and researchers work across extended sessions, and each output becomes the context for the next, while the final product carries a human signature. A test that scores a single response most likely will not reveal the behaviors that emerge under those conditions. This paper describes seven candidate failure patterns identified in exploratory, single-author observation of extended sessions on three commercial AI platforms: recognition without correction, compounding rather than isolation of errors, halo effect from real anchors, unreliable self-explanation, degradation across long sessions, exculpatory framing under confrontation, and sycophancy and confirmation bias amplification. Several are consistent with findings already established in the machine learning literature. Overall, the patterns describe a systemic failure profile that lower hallucination rates do not address because the concern lies in how the system handles errors once they exist. The systemic failure profile carries significant ethical consequences and concerns, since failures cascade to final approval; the duty to verify applies to any domain where a person approves LLM output.
topics: Ethics and Social Impacts of AI

items.title: Foregrounded by AI: What a Sociomaterial Account of Literacy Implies for Postdigital Design Orientations
items.abstract: Abstract This article argues that Large Language Models (LLMs) reveal literacy’s sociomaterial character: that it is constituted within more-than-human assemblages of people, texts, technologies, practices, and infrastructures, rather than in the cognitive capacity of the individual. Rather than asking what new literacies Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) demands, it asks what LLMs reveal about literacy itself. This analysis draws on the sociomaterial tradition in science and technology studies, including actor-network theory, spatial perspectives, and postdigital literacy research. It reconceptualises literacy as emergent practice within assemblages, arguing that competence frameworks, by centring the individual, cannot register the distributed, infrastructural, and nonhuman dimensions of literacy that this shift makes visible. From this analysis, three design orientations for postdigital literacy environments are derived: making assemblages visible, sustaining fluid literacy spaces, and preserving conditions for critical reflexivity. The article concludes by arguing that these orientations carry political as well as pedagogical stakes, since current AI assemblages risk amplifying existing educational inequalities rather than benefiting all learners equally.

items.title: Foundation model for particle collision data analysis
items.abstract: Abstract Data-intensive collider experiments increasingly require models that transfer across high-dimensional, partially observed measurements, yet most analyses still optimize separate models for each task. Here, to address this bottleneck, we introduce EVENET, an event-level foundation model pretrained on 500 million simulated collision events using self-supervised learning and physics-informed supervision. The model constructs a shared particle-cloud representation from the variable-length set of physics objects in each event. Across searches for heavy resonances and exotic Higgs decays, EVENET outperforms both established and state-of-the-art baselines, particularly in low-statistics regimes. We validate transfer to experimental data by rediscovering the ϒ meson in CMS Open Data. The pretrained model also supports precise extraction of quantum-correlation observables that remain stable under the tested systematic variations. Together, these results establish a reusable backbone for diverse collider analyses, improving downstream adaptation after a substantial one-time pretraining investment.
